title: [Market Rider] PSE’s 2027 rebalancing: Will it unlock broader market activity?
summary: The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi.

blocks.text: The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi.

In the search for new catalysts that could lead to unlocking broader market activity and growth, the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) is implementing its biggest index management overhaul since 2011 starting with the February 2027 rebalancing, using the whole-year trading data of 2026.
The revised framework applies to the PSEi, PSE MidCap, PSE Dividend Yield, and sector indices. (READ: What is the PSEi, and why does it matter?)

Unveiled last July, the new rebalancing framework radically departs from the pure market cap methodology by introducing three core changes in the rules for eligibility and liquidity for inclusion in the bourse’s index as it shifts toward free-float trading velocity.

As evaluated, many of our large conglomerates have a high total valuation, but a huge portion of their shares are locked up with founding families or strategic insiders. Under the old rules, a large company could enter or stay in the PSEi simply because of its sheer size and overall peso trading volume, even if its actual public float rarely changed hands.

The first of the three pivotal changes made in the rule is that the PSE instituted a 98% cumulative market capitalization screen. Before even undergoing liquidity evaluations, companies must fall within the top 98% of cumulative total market capitalization among eligible securities. This also effectively filters out the exchange’s smallest listed names from the outset.

Second, the exchange replaced its legacy single liquidity metric with a rigorous dual liquidity test combining the Median Trading Activity Ratio (MTAR) and Monthly Average Daily Value Turnover (MADV). MTAR measures how fast a stock’s publicly available shares are being bought and sold relative to its size, rather than just looking at the raw amounts of pesos traded, while MADV is a liquidity metric that measures the average monetary value of a stock traded per day over a given month.

For the PSEi, MidCap, and Dividend Yield indices, prospective entrants must achieve an MTAR of at least 15%, whereas existing constituents need 10% to retain their spots, a buffer designed to prevent excessive index turnover while sector indices require 7%. Simultaneously, both new and current members of the primary indices must rank in the top 25% of all listed stocks by MADV for at least nine of the 12 months in 2026. For sector indices, the bar is looser. A stock only needs to rank in the top half by daily traded value in at least eight of the 12 months.

Third, the PSE introduced a P250-billion mega-cap float carve-out. While the standard minimum public float remains 20%, corporate giants valued at P250 billion or more can now qualify with a 15% float, provided they satisfy all liquidity tests.

blocks.text: Despite these sweeping updates, several foundational eligibility rules remain intact for the 30-member PSEi. Companies must still maintain a PSE Main Board listing tenure of at least 12 months, or six months for early inclusion if they rank among the top 25 firms by market value.

Once candidates clear the market cap screen, public float minimum, and dual liquidity filters, the top 30 eligible companies ranked by full market capitalization secure their places in the index. Furthermore, the exchange retains its semi-annual rebalancing cadence every February and August.

Ultimately, these revisions carry profound implications for market participants. Under the 2011 framework, tightly held conglomerates could qualify through size and sporadic block trades, creating liquidity bottlenecks for institutional funds trying to execute large orders without distorting prices.

The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi. A company can be worth hundreds of billions of pesos, but if its public shares sit idle without regular trading turnover, it risks being dropped from the benchmark index. Shares need to trade under the new rules.

For domestic institutional investors, including Unit Investment Trust Funds (UITFs), mutual funds, pension systems, and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), enforcing MTAR reduces execution friction and tracking error. Because trading large institutional blocks in large-cap stocks with tightly held floats or thin turnover can push prices sharply against a fund, requiring active trading relative to free float ensures deeper tradable liquidity during rebalances. This allows funds to buy newly added and sell deleted index stocks cleanly at or near benchmark prices and weights, preventing their returns from diverging from the benchmark index. (READ: EXPLAINER: How mutual funds and UITFs make investing beginner-friendly)

Additionally, the P250-billion carve-out creates an immediate pathway into the PSEi for tightly held utility giants. Conversely, the strict nine-month MADV requirement mathematically delays late-2026 mega-IPOs like Mynt (GCash) from immediate entry, ensuring that new additions prove sustained trading depth before attracting passive institutional capital.

By transitioning from static size metrics toward dynamic free-float trading velocity, the PSE is aligning domestic index construction with international institutional standards and mitigate structural illiquidity — standards that is followed by major global stock indexes like the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) index and the Financial Times Stock Exchange Russell (FTSE Russell) index. – Rappler.com
